# Finite Population Correction {#sec-finite-population-correction}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Identify the assumptions supporting FPC.
- Distinguish finite-population precision from finite-clinic recruitment.
:::

## The idea

Finite population correction is relevant when estimating features of an explicitly finite population under an appropriate sampling-without-replacement design. For simple random sampling without replacement, a conventional first approximation adjusts an independently computed planning sample size $n_0$ using $n_{FPC}=n_0/[1+(n_0-1)/N]$. The planning target and exact variance convention should be checked before applying it.

## When and how to apply it

FPC becomes meaningful as the sampling fraction grows. It is not automatically suitable for cluster sampling, repeated observations, a clinical trial or inference to future patients. If the sampling unit is an institution rather than an individual, the finite population must be defined at the correct level.

## Formula at a glance

$$
n_{FPC}=\frac{n_0}{1+(n_0-1)/N}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
An illustrative finite registry of $N=1000$ eligible workers and uncorrected $n_0=384.16$ leads to a corrected planning value near 278. That differs from Taro Yamane because the approaches begin with different assumptions and approximations.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
N <- 1000; n0 <- 1.96^2 * .5 * .5 / .05^2
n_fpc <- n0 / (1 + (n0 - 1)/N)
ceiling(n_fpc)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not enter “annual OPD attendance” as $N$ unless that quantity truly represents the finite population being sampled.
:::
